newsitem.title: USA: Cruise lines aim marketing at shorter trips.
newsitem.headline: Cruise lines aim marketing at shorter trips.

text.p: With the winter vacation season underway, a growing fleet of cruise ships is set to ferry passengers on the kind of vacations once enjoyed only by the wealthy.

The heightened competition -- and the need to fill all of those new ships -- is leading to a spate of television commercials showing cruise ships gliding effortlessly through sunny tropical seas. With more trips, there is an increased need to boost the reach and frequency of advertising.
"There is a public demand for shorter and more frequent trips," said Adam Goldstein, vice president for marketing at Royal Caribbean Lines. "This gives us the opportunity to pioneer some new routes."
But, nothing, it seems, comes easy. With more trips, there is more pressure to sell more passages, "an entirely different sort of marketing challenge," Goldstein said.
The lines are increasingly promoting the value they offer on their cruises.
"Cruising today is a terrific value," says Vicki Freed, Carnival Lines' senior vice president for sales and marketing.

"We're selling 1996 and 1997 cruises at 1982 rates. It's true. There's a lot of new capacity on the market but the new ships are more efficient to run so that it's possible to make a profit from relatively low prices."

Freed argues that the real competition in the cruise-line industry is not among the main players but against such vacation attractions as Las Vegas and DisneyWorld in Orlando, Fla. The cruise business has been flat the last couple of years, but Freed sees room to grow.

"Our total cruise industry only gets about 4.6 million customers a year while Las Vegas draws 28 million and Orlando gets 40 million," she says. "Certainly, the Orlando visitors could be ours. We offer fun, entertainment, excitement and lots of sun, too, and at very reasonable prices."

Goldstein, whose Royal Caribbean is an arch-rival to Carnival Cruises, said that he "agrees completely. There's no benefit to our competing with one another. We have to become a mainstream vacation choice. ... So, it's really a matter of cruise vacations competing with land vacations."

That may well be. But within the cruise industry, there is plenty of evidence of brand competition. Both Carnival Cruise Lines and Royal Caribbean Cruises have increased their ad budgets this year and are vying for short, three- or four-night Caribbean trips.
A fierce competition is underway between Holland America, Carnival's second-largest line, and Princess Cruises for the increasingly popular Alaska trip and accompanying railway tour.

Not to be outdone by Carnival or Royal Carribean, Celebrity Cruises has launched its newest ship, Galaxy, for seven-night cruises to the Western Caribbean and also will place it in the Alaska run next May.

But it is Carnival, founded 25 years ago by Ted Arison, which is both the largest and most diversified of the cruise lines. It has four distinct price brackets starting with the Carnival group ($150 a person per day) and moving up to Holland America ($225-$250), the smaller Windstar ships ($350-$400) and the suites-only Seabourn line ($700-$800).

"We have 11 ships sailing 50 weeks a year to different destinations," noted Freed of Carnival. "We do not focus our advertising on specific sailing dates but on the cruise as the best vacation value. We are spending more this year, heavily on television as our mainstay with newspapers secondary."

She said the line has spent $6 million this year for advertising alone in People magazine in "a departure from our traditional advertising in the travel media. We think that People gives us a different audience because it is a 'fun' publication." Carnival's ad agency is HMS in Miami.

Royal Caribbean began in the fall to promote bookings for the 1997 first quarter, stressing cruises to the Caribbean or Panama Canal rather than any particular cruise dates "as opposed to some other lines which get very specific about prices on certain dates."
The company concentrates its advertising, which is handled by the McKinney & Silver agency in Raleigh, N.C., in the travel sections of Sunday papers, "which are most tactical for us."
For Royal Caribbean, also based in Miami, it is making a major effort to expand the number of its three-and four-nite bookings to the Caribbean and also venture into some new routes.
